sections.body_md: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a matrix only stretches. The stretch factor is the eigenvalue: \(Av = \lambda v\). The zero vector satisfies that equation for every number, so it is excluded. For a 2 by 2 matrix the eigenvalues are the roots of a quadratic built from the trace and the determinant.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: The characteristic polynomial is \(\det(\lambda I - A)\). For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}\), \[ \lambda^2 - (p + s)\lambda + (ps - qr) = 0. \] The sum of the roots is the trace. The product of the roots is the determinant. When a full set of eigenvectors exists they are the columns of an invertible \(P\), and \[ A = P D P^{-1} \] with the eigenvalues on the diagonal of \(D\). A triangular matrix lists its eigenvalues on its own diagonal.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take the diagonal matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(13, 15)\). The characteristic polynomial is \((\lambda - 13)(\lambda - 15)\). The eigenvalues are 13 and 15, which are the diagonal entries. The first standard basis vector is an eigenvector for 13, and the second is an eigenvector for 15. The eigenvector matrix can be the identity, and \(D\) holds 13 and 15. A matrix similar to this one has the same eigenvalues. Its eigenvectors are those two directions written in the other coordinates.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Adding the trace instead of subtracting it in \(\det(\lambda I - A)\).
- Treating a repeated eigenvalue as two eigenvectors. A single off-diagonal 1 above a repeated diagonal entry leaves only one eigenvector direction.
- Reading an off-diagonal entry of a triangular matrix as an eigenvalue.
- Expecting a change of coordinates to change the eigenvalues. It changes the coordinates of the eigenvectors.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A mode of a linear system is \(e^{\lambda t} v\), and the time constant is read from the real part. A real symmetric matrix has orthonormal eigenvectors and the factorization \(A = U D U^T\). A symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when every one of these eigenvalues is positive.
